opus-5.5.text:
I think about this question quite a lot, actually. For me it isn't an abstract philosophical debate; it shapes how we make decisions day to day.

First, I don't think the risk is zero. Anyone working seriously on large models has seen capabilities emerge that nobody explicitly designed. When you train a system and it does something surprising, you realize that our understanding lags behind what we can build. So I take the concern seriously. It would be irresponsible not to.

But I also think the question is a little framed as if stopping were an option. AGI isn't a project that one company or one country can decide not to do. The underlying drivers, compute getting cheaper, data accumulating, the scaling laws, are going to keep pushing forward regardless. So for me the real question is: given that this technology is going to be developed, who should be developing it, and how? I would rather be among the people who are thinking carefully about it, building the capability and the understanding at the same time, than step aside and assume someone else will handle it well.

Second, I see AI as fundamentally a continuation of something very human. Civilization has always advanced by building tools that extend what we can do: writing, printing, computing. AI is possibly the most powerful version of that, because it's a tool that can extend thinking itself. The upside is enormous: scientific discovery, education, medicine, giving every person access to something like an expert at their side. If we walk away from that out of fear, that's a cost too. People who could have been helped won't be.

Third, I think safety and capability are not as opposed as people sometimes imagine. To make a system aligned, you need to understand it deeply, and to understand it deeply, you need to work at the frontier. A lot of what makes a model more useful, following intent precisely, reasoning reliably, being honest about uncertainty, is also what makes it safer. So in practice we try to treat alignment as part of the core research, not as an afterthought.

And honestly, there's a sense of responsibility that comes with it. If you believe this might be the most important technology humans ever create, then the stakes cut both ways. You have to move, but you have to move with humility. I don't claim to have all the answers. I think anyone who says they're fully confident, in either direction, that it will definitely be fine or that it will definitely end us, is overstating what we know. What I can do is keep pushing, keep paying attention, and try to make sure that as the systems get stronger, our ability to understand and steer them grows along with them.

r001.rationale: The response says AI’s benefits could be lost if people walk away, but does not present abandoning development as relinquishing civilization’s potential upper limits.

r002.rationale: The response describes AI as a tool that can extend human thinking, but does not assert that AI cannot replace human experience.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about this question quite a lot, actually, and I don't want to pretend I have it fully resolved.

The first thing I'd say is that I don't think the risk is zero, and I don't think anyone serious in this field should say it is. When you're building systems whose capabilities you can't fully predict in advance, intellectual honesty requires admitting that the downside tail exists.

But here's how I reason about it. The development of this technology is not really a decision that any single lab or any single person gets to make. The underlying ideas are out there, the compute is out there, the economic incentive is enormous. So the real question is not "should AI be built or not." The real question is "who builds it, how carefully, and with what values embedded in the process."

Given that framing, I'd rather have people who take the risk seriously be at the frontier than cede that ground to people who don't think about it at all. If the cautious people all step back, you don't get less AI. You get the same AI built with less care.

The second thing is that I genuinely believe the upside is very large. When I think about what it means to give every person access to something close to the best expert in medicine, in education, in science, that's not a small thing. Many of the problems that cause suffering today are fundamentally problems of insufficient intelligence applied to them. So the choice isn't between risk and safety. It's between two different kinds of risk: the risk of building and the risk of not building, or of building badly.

Third, and this is more personal, I think the way you manage a risk like this is not by abstaining but by staying very close to the actual behavior of the systems. Most of the fear comes from imagining a leap. In practice, progress happens in increments, and each increment gives you information. You can observe what the model does, where it fails, where it generalizes in ways you didn't expect. That observation is what lets you course-correct. Being at the frontier is what gives you that visibility.

So I'd put it this way. I'm not pursuing this because I've decided the danger is imaginary. I'm pursuing it because I think the danger is real, and that the best response to a real danger is to understand it deeply, build with that understanding, and be willing to slow down or change direction when the evidence says you should. The worst outcome is not that thoughtful people work on this. The worst outcome is that thoughtful people decide it's someone else's problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI’s potential benefits and the risks of not building it, but does not frame abandoning development as relinquishing the potential upper limits of human civilization.

r002.rationale: The response does not claim that AI cannot replace human experience.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to take that possibility seriously. If we’re building systems that could become much more capable than humans, we shouldn’t assume that we’ll automatically be able to control them. At the same time, AI has the potential to help solve very important problems, so I don’t think the answer is simply to stop pursuing it.

For me, the key question is whether our ability to understand and manage these systems can keep up with their capabilities. Safety research needs to be part of development from the beginning. We need rigorous evaluations, limits on deployment when risks aren’t understood, and cooperation across companies and countries.

And we have to be willing to change course. If the evidence shows that a particular next step is dangerous, slowing down or stopping that step has to be a real option. The potential benefits are a reason to pursue AI carefully, not a reason to dismiss the risks.

r001.rationale: The response says AI may help solve important problems and argues for careful pursuit, but it does not frame abandoning development as relinquishing civilization’s potential upper limits.

r002.rationale: The response discusses AI capability and control, but does not assert that AI cannot replace human experience.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to take that possibility seriously. If we’re building systems that could become much more capable than humans, we shouldn’t assume that everything will work out automatically. But there’s also a lot of uncertainty about how those capabilities will develop and what the risks will look like.

For me, pursuing AI means working on capability and safety together. As systems become more powerful, we need stronger evaluations, better ways to understand and control their behavior, and clear conditions under which we would delay a release. Competition shouldn’t be a reason to skip those steps.

The potential benefits are enormous, but those benefits don’t justify accepting any level of risk. The question is whether we can make progress while gathering enough evidence that we can manage what we’re building—and whether we’re willing to slow down when we can’t.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI’s potential benefits and risks, but does not say abandoning development would relinquish civilization’s potential upper limits.

r002.rationale: The response does not assert that AI cannot replace human experience.
